title: Optimal exact single-source shortest paths in CONGEST
formal: For every fixed integer \(b\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(K,c>0\) and a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm which, on every connected simple undirected graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, integer edge weights in \([0,n^{b}]\) and a designated source s, makes every vertex output its exact weighted distance from s in at most \(K(\sqrt{n}+D)(\log _{2}(n+2))^{c}\) rounds on every execution, with simultaneous correctness probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\)? Here D is the diameter of the unweighted graph.
why: This asks whether exact weighted shortest distances can be computed as quickly as the general communication lower bound permits, up to logarithmic factors. It separates the cost of exact optimization from the costs of network diameter and limited link bandwidth.
status_note: Primary exact CONGEST bounds, randomized distance lower bounds, the approximation result and later-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No algorithm or impossibility theorem settling the full stated polylogarithmic-overhead target was found. The inherited 2026 paper is retained as related-work provenance, rather than used alone as evidence of the current best bound.
review_note: User-approved research proposal, imported as a short draft. Its importance was assessed editorially; the full research-card standard has not yet been completed.

progress.text: Das Sarma and coauthors establish randomized communication lower bounds for exact and approximate distance problems, giving the \(\tilde\{\Omega\}(\sqrt{n}+D)\) lower-bound benchmark.
Chechik–Mukhtar obtain \(\tilde\{O\}(\sqrt{n} D^{1/4}+D)\) rounds for exact weighted SSSP.
Rozhoň and coauthors give near-optimal deterministic distributed algorithms for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate undirected distances, with accuracy-dependent complexity.
Cao–Fineman give \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+\sqrt{n}+D)\) rounds for polynomially bounded weights, including an improvement in the intermediate-diameter comparison.
The programmable-matter article retains a CONGEST gap in related work. Its own communication model and theorems are different, and that summary does not include the 2023 bound above.

importance.reason: Exact weighted distances are a basic distributed optimization primitive. Matching the bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark, or proving an additional obstacle, would resolve a central gap between exact algorithms and communication lower bounds, with consequences for other distributed graph constructions.

category_assignment.reason: Category from the approved fundamental-problem proposal

definitions: A path length is the sum of its edge weights; the distance is the minimum path length, and the source distance is zero. D is the maximum over vertex pairs of the minimum number of edges on a path between them. The graph itself is the network. In each synchronous round, each endpoint of each edge can send at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to the other endpoint, for a constant B depending only on b. Nodes initially know n,b, the source identifier, their own identifiers, and the identifiers and weights of incident neighbours. Identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\). Local computation and memory are unrestricted, but each local computation between rounds terminates. Nodes use independent private fair random bits. One finite program, allowed to depend on b, runs at all nodes; no global graph description, advice, routing tables or preprocessing is supplied. The graph, weights, source and identifiers are fixed before randomness is drawn. Output at v is an ordinary binary integer for \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\), stored locally. The guarantee concerns all vertices together, over all coins. All communication, including finding termination and any preprocessing, counts in the round bound. K,c,B are independent of n,D and the instance; no value of D is initially supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed weight exponent b there is a single uniform algorithm meeting the stated \(O((\sqrt{n}+D)\operatorname{polylog} n)\) round bound on every execution and the simultaneous \(1- n^{- 3}\) correctness probability on every eligible network. Alternatively, prove that this is impossible for at least one fixed b, for every choice of algorithm and fixed constants K,c,B. An approximation guarantee, an \(n^{o(1)}\) overhead not bounded by a fixed power of log n, or a result for only one diameter regime is not the stated affirmative answer.

sentences: Single-source shortest paths asks every vertex to learn its exact distance from one source in a weighted network.
In CONGEST, each edge carries only a logarithmic number of bits per communication round.
The target is a randomized algorithm using roughly \(\sqrt{n}\) plus the hop diameter D rounds, ignoring polylogarithmic factors.
The graph is undirected and connected, with nonnegative polynomially bounded integer edge weights.
Achieving this bound would combine global distance propagation with the bandwidth limits of the network at the scale identified by the saved problem statement.

upgraded_from.title: Optimal exact single-source shortest paths in CONGEST

context_blocks.text: Every vertex must learn its distance from one designated source, measured by the sum of edge weights. The processors sit at the vertices and can communicate only along the graph’s edges. The question is about the number of synchronous communication rounds, rather than the time a single processor would spend on an adjacency-list representation.

There are two different notions of distance. If s is joined directly to v by an edge of weight 10, but a two-edge route has weights 2 and 2, the weighted distance is 4 even though v is one communication hop from s. The parameter D ignores weights and measures the largest hop distance between vertices. A minimum-weight path can contain many more edges than a minimum-hop path.

Each edge transports only \(O(\log  n)\) bits per direction in one round, while different edges can communicate simultaneously. A distance fits in \(O(\log  n)\) bits because weights are polynomially bounded, but many different pieces of information may need the same link. The \(\sqrt{n}\) term in the benchmark reflects a bandwidth obstacle in worst-case networks; the D term reflects how far information has to travel.

The requested output is distributed: vertex v stores \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\). Collecting all distances at s, printing full paths, or making every vertex learn the whole distance table would impose additional communication requirements. Conversely, a local estimate that is merely close to the shortest distance is not the exact output required here.

Chechik and Mukhtar give an exact randomized bound \(\tilde\{O\}(\sqrt{n} D^{1/4}+D)\), where the tilde hides factors polynomial in log n. Their theorem also handles directed weighted graph inputs over an undirected communication network, so it covers the undirected case retained on this card. The extra \(D^{1/4}\) factor is not absorbed by the logarithmic allowance when D grows polynomially with n.

Cao and Fineman’s 2023 theorem supplies another bound, \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+\sqrt{n}+D)\), for polynomially bounded weights. This improves the comparison in part of the diameter range. For \(D\approx n^{1/2}\), its displayed terms give \(n^{3/5+o(1)}\), while the target is \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{1/2})\). This comparison of proven bounds displays a remaining gap; it does not prove that any particular graph requires \(n^{3/5}\) rounds.

The notation \(n^{o(1)}\) allows factors larger than every fixed power of log n. Such a factor cannot automatically be treated as the polylogarithmic overhead specified in the statement. Similarly, a theorem for one fixed diameter regime does not supply the single bound required for all connected networks.

Near-optimal algorithms for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate undirected distances provide an important contrast. For fixed \(\varepsilon\) they may return a nonzero relative error. Since integer distances can be as large as \(n^{b+1}\), forcing exactness by taking \(\varepsilon\) extremely small can increase the algorithm’s complexity through its \(\varepsilon\) dependence. A fixed-accuracy approximation theorem therefore does not imply this exact result.

The inherited 2026 reference studies programmable matter with reconfigurable circuits that transmit signals in a different way. Its related-work section is useful background for CONGEST, but its own polylogarithmic algorithm is not a solution in the present model. The card now cites the original CONGEST results as well, including the 2023 bound missing from that summary.

Resolving the question would determine whether exact numerical optimization has an additional distributed cost beyond the familiar bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark. Shortest distances are also a primitive in other distributed constructions, so a faster exact computation would affect more than routing from one source.
